### Treatment Overview

Treatment overview:

Dental Consultation is a dental procedure or care pathway that provides a focused assessment of a new concern, second-opinion request or proposed treatment before care is recommended. It may be considered for concerns including tooth pain, sensitivity, damaged teeth, gum concerns, missing teeth, bite symptoms, aesthetic questions, treatment-planning needs. The exact indication must be confirmed through history-taking, clinical examination and any justified diagnostic records.

Assessment commonly reviews symptoms, dental and medical history, medicines, allergies, oral hygiene, gum health, remaining tooth structure, bite and patient priorities. Where relevant, the clinician may discuss focused consultation, comprehensive new-patient assessment, second opinion, referral-oriented consultation. Tests, photographs, scans or dental radiographs should be requested only when they are clinically justified and available at the clinic.

The appointment is problem-led and may end with reassurance, monitoring, preventive advice, further investigation, a staged treatment plan or referral. It does not guarantee a diagnosis or a particular procedure at the first visit.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Examination may not establish a final diagnosis at the first visit; further tests, monitoring or referral can be required. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

Website information cannot diagnose an individual or confirm suitability. A registered dental practitioner must review the clinical findings before treatment is recommended, and clinic-specific equipment, materials, practitioner availability and protocols must be verified before this page is published.

## Treatment Details

### Typical Appointment Duration

Approximately 30–60 minutes. This is an estimate rather than a guaranteed appointment length.

### Typical Number of Visits

Usually one initial visit; further diagnostic or planning visits may be required. The final sequence depends on diagnostic findings, response to treatment and the agreed plan.

### Anaesthesia or Sedation

Anaesthesia is usually unnecessary for assessment alone. Local anaesthesia may be used for a separately consented diagnostic or treatment procedure. Sedation availability must be confirmed directly with the clinic. No sedation service is claimed for Titanium Roots unless availability is separately verified.

### Benefits

* Title: Focused assessment
* Description: Investigates the reason for attendance rather than assuming a diagnosis from symptoms alone.
* Sort order: 1

* Title: Informed planning
* Description: Supports discussion of findings, reasonable options, limitations, risks and alternatives before treatment.
* Sort order: 2

* Title: Medical-history review
* Description: Identifies health conditions, medicines, allergies and previous experiences that may affect dental care.
* Sort order: 3

* Title: Appropriate diagnostics
* Description: Allows tests or images to be selected according to clinical need rather than used automatically.
* Sort order: 4

* Title: Opportunity for questions
* Description: Creates time to clarify priorities, expected stages, maintenance and factors affecting cost.
* Sort order: 5

* Title: Referral when appropriate
* Description: May identify a need for specialist dental assessment, medical input or additional investigation.
* Sort order: 6

### Expected Outcome

The intended outcome is to provides a focused assessment of a new concern, second-opinion request or proposed treatment before care is recommended within the biological and technical limits identified during assessment. Improvement may relate to health, comfort, function, appearance or maintenance, depending on the purpose of dental consultation.

Results are not guaranteed. Examination may not establish a final diagnosis at the first visit; further tests, monitoring or referral can be required. The outcome depends on diagnosis, anatomy, material or appliance selection, clinician technique, oral hygiene, general health, habits, attendance and long-term maintenance. Additional treatment, repair, review or referral may be required.

### Expected Longevity

The findings remain relevant only while symptoms, oral condition, medical history and diagnostic information remain substantially unchanged.

For dental consultation, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving tooth pain, sensitivity, damaged teeth, gum concerns, missing teeth, bite symptoms, aesthetic questions, treatment-planning needs.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Inability to provide informed consent without appropriate support — arrange a legally valid decision-making process.
* Acute medical instability — a reason to delay elective assessment or obtain medical clearance.
* Active contagious illness — a reason to postpone a non-urgent appointment according to infection-control advice.
* Incomplete medicine or allergy information — may limit the safety of immediate recommendations.
* Severe anxiety or additional needs — may require a longer appointment, adjustments or another care setting.
* Potentially serious symptoms — may require urgent medical or specialist assessment rather than routine consultation.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Alternative Treatments

* **Routine Dental Check-up**  
  A diagnostic or preventive assessment used when further examination is needed before selecting a procedure.

* **Digital Dental X-Rays**

## Patient Journey

### Before-Treatment Preparation

* Provide a complete dental and medical history, current medicines and known allergies.
* Describe the concerns related to dental consultation, including timing, triggers and previous treatment.
* Allow a clinical examination and only those diagnostic records that are justified.
* Discuss reasonable alternatives, expected benefits, recognised risks and the option of no immediate treatment.
* Address active decay, gum disease or poor plaque control before elective definitive care where relevant.
* Inform the clinician about pregnancy, bleeding risk, smoking or nicotine use and previous treatment complications.
* Clarify appointment sequence, aftercare, maintenance responsibilities and factors affecting cost.
* Provide informed consent only after questions have been answered.

### Procedure Steps

A typical treatment pathway may include:

1. **Reason for attendance**  
   The clinician records the concern, its timing, severity, triggers and the outcome the patient hopes to achieve.

2. **Medical and dental history**  
   Health conditions, medicines, allergies, previous care and relevant risk factors are reviewed.

3. **Clinical examination**  
   The teeth, gums, bite, jaw and oral tissues are examined according to the presenting concern.

4. **Diagnostic tests**  
   Appropriate chairside tests are selected to clarify the likely source and severity of the problem.

5. **Imaging decision**  
   Existing records are reviewed and new images are requested only where the expected diagnostic benefit justifies them.

6. **Findings discussion**  
   The clinician explains what can and cannot be concluded from the available evidence.

7. **Options and consent**  
   Reasonable monitoring, preventive, restorative, surgical or referral options are compared.

8. **Next-step plan**  
   Further records, treatment, review or referral appointments are arranged where appropriate.

### Recovery and Downtime

A consultation or examination usually has no physical downtime. Temporary tenderness may occur if an already painful tooth, inflamed gum or jaw area is examined. Normal activity can usually resume immediately unless a separate procedure or local anaesthesia is provided.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

### Risks and Limitations

A consultation may not establish a final diagnosis at the first visit; hidden disease, evolving symptoms or incomplete records can require additional tests or review. Examination may not establish a final diagnosis at the first visit; further tests, monitoring or referral can be required.

The procedure may not achieve every intended functional or aesthetic objective. Biological response, anatomy, material limitations, patient cooperation and maintenance affect results. Future review, repair, retreatment, replacement or referral may be required.

### Aftercare

* Follow the personalised advice provided.
* Arrange recommended diagnostic, review or treatment appointments.
* Obtain previous records or medical clearance if requested.
* Monitor symptoms and note meaningful changes.
* Continue routine brushing and interdental cleaning.
* Do not start, stop or change prescribed medicines without relevant clinical advice.
* Seek reassessment if symptoms worsen before the planned review.

### When to Contact the Clinic

Contact the treating clinic for:

* Increasing pain rather than gradual improvement.
* Persistent or rapidly increasing swelling.
* Fever, discharge, a bad taste or other signs of infection.
* Prolonged or difficult-to-control bleeding.
* A loose, broken or lost restoration, appliance or prosthesis.
* A bite that feels significantly abnormal.
* Numbness or altered sensation lasting longer than expected.

Rapidly increasing facial swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe trauma, fever with spreading infection or uncontrolled bleeding may require urgent medical or dental care. This does not imply that Titanium Roots provides emergency or 24-hour services.

### When to Book a Consultation

Arrange a professional assessment when concerns involving tooth pain, sensitivity, damaged teeth, gum concerns, missing teeth, bite symptoms, aesthetic questions, treatment-planning needs are present, when symptoms persist or when you want to understand whether dental consultation is appropriate. A dentist must examine the relevant teeth, gums, bite or supporting tissues before recommending care. Contact Titanium Roots Dental Clinic to arrange a consultation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### FAQ 1

Question: What is Dental Consultation?

Answer:

Dental Consultation provides a focused assessment of a new concern, second-opinion request or proposed treatment before care is recommended. It may be considered for tooth pain, sensitivity, damaged teeth, gum concerns, missing teeth, bite symptoms, aesthetic questions, treatment-planning needs, but the name of a treatment does not confirm that it is suitable for a particular person. The dentist must review symptoms, medical and dental history, clinical findings and any justified diagnostic records. The recommended approach may include focused consultation, comprehensive new-patient assessment, second opinion, referral-oriented consultation.

### FAQ 2

Question: Is dental consultation painful?

Answer:

Comfort varies with the condition being treated and the steps required. Anaesthesia is usually unnecessary for assessment alone. Local anaesthesia may be used for a separately consented diagnostic or treatment procedure. Sedation availability must be confirmed directly with the clinic. Pressure, vibration, temporary tenderness or sensitivity may still occur, and no responsible page can promise completely painless care. Tell the treating clinician about anxiety, previous difficult experiences or discomfort so that the procedure and support can be adjusted where clinically possible.

### FAQ 3

Question: How long does dental consultation take?

Answer:

A typical estimate is approximately 30–60 minutes, but this is not guaranteed. Time varies with the number of teeth or areas involved, anatomy, disease severity, records, anaesthesia, cooperation, material or appliance selection and whether unexpected findings change the plan. Complex treatment should not be shortened merely to meet an advertised appointment time.

### FAQ 4

Question: How many visits are required for dental consultation?

Answer:

Usually one initial visit; further diagnostic or planning visits may be required. Additional visits may be needed for diagnostic records, disease stabilisation, laboratory stages, healing, adjustment, review or management of complications. The dentist should explain the anticipated sequence after examination, while making clear that the plan can change if clinical findings or healing differ from expectations.

### FAQ 5

Question: Who may be suitable for dental consultation?

Answer:

Possible candidates have a confirmed indication involving tooth pain, sensitivity, damaged teeth, gum concerns, missing teeth, bite symptoms, aesthetic questions, treatment-planning needs, acceptable medical and oral-health conditions, and realistic expectations about benefits and limitations. Suitability may also depend on age, growth, tooth structure, gum or bone support, hygiene, smoking, medicines and ability to attend maintenance. A website description cannot replace a clinical assessment.

### FAQ 6

Question: How long do the results of dental consultation last?

Answer:

The findings remain relevant only while symptoms, oral condition, medical history and diagnostic information remain substantially unchanged. Individual results vary. Oral hygiene, diet, general health, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, grinding, bite forces, material wear and attendance for maintenance can alter longevity. Even a satisfactory result may later need adjustment, repair, retreatment or replacement.

### FAQ 7

Question: What are the alternatives to dental consultation?

Answer:

Alternatives depend on the diagnosis and may include Routine Dental Check-up, Digital Dental X-Rays, Tooth Sensitivity Treatment. Monitoring or no immediate treatment may also be reasonable in selected situations. Options differ in invasiveness, reversibility, cost, maintenance, appearance and expected function. No one approach is universally superior, so the comparison must be based on the individual findings and informed preferences.

### FAQ 8

Question: What affects the cost of dental consultation?

Answer:

Cost may depend on assessment complexity, the number of teeth or areas, diagnostic imaging, materials, laboratory work, clinician or specialist involvement, anaesthesia, number of visits, additional procedures and maintenance requirements. Titanium Roots has not supplied a verified fee, so the CMS must display “Consultation required” and avoid publishing a numerical amount until formally approved.

### Expected Longevity

Preventive benefit depends on ongoing home care, risk control and attendance at an individualised review interval.

For routine dental check-up, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving early decay, gum inflammation, restoration wear, tooth wear, oral-hygiene needs, asymptomatic oral changes.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Active cavitated disease requiring restorative care — preventive treatment alone may be insufficient.
* Uncontrolled gum disease — requires periodontal assessment alongside preventive measures.
* Allergy or sensitivity to the proposed product — select an alternative material.
* Inability to maintain basic oral hygiene — increases ongoing risk and requires tailored support.
* Medical instability — delay elective care or obtain clearance where relevant.
* Unrealistic expectation that prevention removes all future disease risk — address through informed discussion.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Alternative Treatments

* **Dental Consultation**  
  A diagnostic or preventive assessment used when further examination is needed before selecting a procedure.

* **Teeth Cleaning and Polishing**  
  A gum-health option chosen according to inflammation, pocket depth, attachment, bone support and previous treatment.

* **Digital Dental X-Rays**  
  A clinically relevant alternative or complementary pathway selected after diagnosis and comparison of risks, limitations and maintenance.

* **Professional Fluoride Treatment**  
  A preventive approach that may be more conservative when the tooth or patient remains suitable.

## Patient Journey

### Before-Treatment Preparation

* Provide a complete dental and medical history, current medicines and known allergies.
* Describe the concerns related to routine dental check-up, including timing, triggers and previous treatment.
* Allow a clinical examination and only those diagnostic records that are justified.
* Discuss reasonable alternatives, expected benefits, recognised risks and the option of no immediate treatment.
* Address active decay, gum disease or poor plaque control before elective definitive care where relevant.
* Inform the clinician about pregnancy, bleeding risk, smoking or nicotine use and previous treatment complications.
* Clarify appointment sequence, aftercare, maintenance responsibilities and factors affecting cost.
* Provide informed consent only after questions have been answered.

### Procedure Steps

A typical treatment pathway may include:

1. **Risk assessment**  
   The clinician reviews previous disease, hygiene, diet, fluoride exposure and relevant medical factors.

2. **Clinical examination**  
   Susceptible teeth or surfaces are inspected to confirm whether preventive care is appropriate.

3. **Disease-status check**  
   Active cavitation, gum disease or another condition requiring treatment is identified before prevention proceeds.

4. **Product or technique selection**  
   The preventive material, concentration, surface or method is selected for the individual indication.

5. **Isolation and preparation**  
   The treatment area is cleaned and controlled as required for the selected product.

6. **Application**  
   The preventive material is placed according to its clinical instructions.

7. **Quality check**  
   Coverage, retention or treated surfaces are reviewed.

8. **Home-care and recall**  
   The clinician explains daily care, diet, fluoride use and when the result should be reassessed.

### Recovery and Downtime

Most preventive procedures cause little or no downtime. Temporary taste, surface roughness, mild gum contact or brief sensitivity may occur depending on the product. Eating and drinking instructions vary with the material used and should be followed exactly.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

### Risks and Limitations

Preventive measures reduce risk but cannot guarantee that decay or gum disease will not occur, and treated surfaces still require daily care and monitoring. A normal check-up cannot guarantee that no condition is present or will develop before the next review.

The procedure may not achieve every intended functional or aesthetic objective. Biological response, anatomy, material limitations, patient cooperation and maintenance affect results. Future review, repair, retreatment, replacement or referral may be required.

### Aftercare

* Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste as advised.
* Clean between teeth using an appropriate method.
* Follow dietary advice aimed at reducing frequent sugar exposure.
* Avoid tobacco and areca-nut use.
* Attend the recommended risk-based review.
* Monitor treated surfaces or risk areas for change.
* Use additional fluoride products only when recommended by a clinician.

### When to Contact the Clinic

Contact the treating clinic for:

* Increasing pain rather than gradual improvement.
* Persistent or rapidly increasing swelling.
* Fever, discharge, a bad taste or other signs of infection.
* Prolonged or difficult-to-control bleeding.
* A loose, broken or lost restoration, appliance or prosthesis.
* A bite that feels significantly abnormal.
* Numbness or altered sensation lasting longer than expected.

Rapidly increasing facial swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe trauma, fever with spreading infection or uncontrolled bleeding may require urgent medical or dental care. This does not imply that Titanium Roots provides emergency or 24-hour services.

### When to Book a Consultation

Arrange a professional assessment when concerns involving early decay, gum inflammation, restoration wear, tooth wear, oral-hygiene needs, asymptomatic oral changes are present, when symptoms persist or when you want to understand whether routine dental check-up is appropriate. A dentist must examine the relevant teeth, gums, bite or supporting tissues before recommending care. Contact Titanium Roots Dental Clinic to arrange a consultation.

Answer:

Comfort varies with the condition being treated and the steps required. Preventive assessment commonly requires no anaesthesia. Local anaesthesia may be considered only for a separately planned procedure. Pressure, vibration, temporary tenderness or sensitivity may still occur, and no responsible page can promise completely painless care. Complex treatment should not be shortened merely to meet an advertised appointment time.

### Treatment Overview

Treatment overview:

Teeth Cleaning and Polishing is a dental procedure or care pathway that removes clinically indicated plaque, supragingival calculus and selected external stains while supporting effective home care. It may be considered for concerns including plaque deposits, hardened calculus, external staining, mild local gingival inflammation, difficult-to-clean areas. The exact indication must be confirmed through history-taking, clinical examination and any justified diagnostic records.

Assessment commonly reviews symptoms, dental and medical history, medicines, allergies, oral hygiene, gum health, remaining tooth structure, bite and patient priorities. Where relevant, the clinician may discuss hand scaling, ultrasonic scaling, selective polishing. Tests, photographs, scans or dental radiographs should be requested only when they are clinically justified and available at the clinic.

This is distinct from therapeutic periodontal instrumentation for established periodontitis. If pocketing, attachment loss or bone loss is suspected, a periodontal assessment and different treatment pathway may be required.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Temporary sensitivity, tenderness, mild bleeding and increased visibility of spaces or recession may follow deposit removal. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

Website information cannot diagnose an individual or confirm suitability. A registered dental practitioner must review the clinical findings before treatment is recommended, and clinic-specific equipment, materials, practitioner availability and protocols must be verified before this page is published.

## Treatment Details

### Typical Appointment Duration

Approximately 30–60 minutes. This is an estimate rather than a guaranteed appointment length.

### Typical Number of Visits

Usually one visit; extensive deposits or periodontal disease may require staged care. The final sequence depends on diagnostic findings, response to treatment and the agreed plan.

### Anaesthesia or Sedation

Routine cleaning often needs no anaesthesia. Local anaesthesia may be considered for sensitivity, inflamed tissues or deeper periodontal instrumentation. No sedation service is claimed for Titanium Roots unless availability is separately verified.

### Benefits

* Title: Deposit removal
* Description: Removes clinically indicated plaque and hardened deposits that cannot be fully removed by normal brushing.
* Sort order: 1

* Title: External-stain reduction
* Description: May reduce selected surface stains without changing the intrinsic colour of the teeth.
* Sort order: 2

* Title: Easier home cleaning
* Description: Can make cleaned surfaces easier to maintain with brushing and interdental cleaning.
* Sort order: 3

* Title: Gum-health support
* Description: Reduces local plaque-retentive deposits that may contribute to gum inflammation.
* Sort order: 4

* Title: Hygiene guidance
* Description: Provides an opportunity to identify difficult areas and improve daily cleaning technique.
* Sort order: 5

* Title: Periodontal triage
* Description: May reveal findings that require periodontal assessment rather than routine cleaning.
* Sort order: 6

### Expected Outcome

The intended outcome is to removes clinically indicated plaque, supragingival calculus and selected external stains while supporting effective home care within the biological and technical limits identified during assessment. Improvement may relate to health, comfort, function, appearance or maintenance, depending on the purpose of teeth cleaning and polishing.

Results are not guaranteed. Temporary sensitivity, tenderness, mild bleeding and increased visibility of spaces or recession may follow deposit removal. The outcome depends on diagnosis, anatomy, material or appliance selection, clinician technique, oral hygiene, general health, habits, attendance and long-term maintenance. Additional treatment, repair, review or referral may be required.

### Expected Longevity

Plaque begins to reform quickly. Calculus and stains recur at different rates according to oral hygiene, saliva, diet, tobacco exposure and individual susceptibility.

For teeth cleaning and polishing, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving plaque deposits, hardened calculus, external staining, mild local gingival inflammation, difficult-to-clean areas.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Established periodontitis — may require scaling and root planing or specialist periodontal care rather than routine cleaning.
* Uncontrolled bleeding disorder — a relative contraindication requiring medical and dental planning.
* Severe oral ulceration, acute infection or pain — assess and manage the cause before elective instrumentation.
* Active contagious respiratory illness — postpone non-urgent aerosol-generating care.
* Known sensitivity to polishing products or materials — use suitable alternatives.
* Complex implants or restorations — require material-appropriate instruments and trained care.
* Severe sensitivity — may require local anaesthesia, staged care or a modified technique.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Procedure Steps

1. **Oral and gum assessment**

2. **Treatment selection**  
   Routine cleaning is confirmed as appropriate or a periodontal pathway is recommended.

3. **Deposit removal**  
   Hand instruments, powered scaling or a suitable combination may remove accessible calculus.

4. **Plaque removal**  
   Remaining soft deposits are cleaned from suitable tooth and restoration surfaces.

5. **Selective polishing**  
   Polishing is used only where surface-stain reduction or finishing is indicated.

6. **Rinsing and inspection**  
   The mouth is rinsed and cleaned surfaces are checked.

7. **Hygiene instruction**  
   Difficult areas and suitable brushing or interdental methods are discussed.

8. **Recall planning**  
   Future review is based on gum health, deposit recurrence and individual risk.

### Recovery and Downtime

Normal activity can usually resume immediately. Mild gum tenderness, slight bleeding and temporary sensitivity to cold may occur, especially when deposits or inflammation were present. Recovery varies with the amount and depth of cleaning.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

Temporary sensitivity, gum tenderness and slight bleeding may occur; routine cleaning does not treat advanced periodontal pockets or intrinsic tooth colour. Temporary sensitivity, tenderness, mild bleeding and increased visibility of spaces or recession may follow deposit removal.

* Use a soft toothbrush if gums feel temporarily tender.
* Avoid tobacco use and reduce frequent staining exposures.
* Follow sensitivity advice from the treating clinician.
* Attend periodontal assessment if deeper gum findings were identified.
* Do not attempt to scrape calculus with sharp objects.

Possible candidates have a confirmed indication involving plaque deposits, hardened calculus, external staining, mild local gingival inflammation, difficult-to-clean areas, acceptable medical and oral-health conditions, and realistic expectations about benefits and limitations. Suitability may also depend on age, growth, tooth structure, gum or bone support, hygiene, smoking, medicines and ability to attend maintenance. A website description cannot replace a clinical assessment.

### FAQ 6

Question: How long do the results of teeth cleaning and polishing last?

Answer:

Plaque begins to reform quickly. Calculus and stains recur at different rates according to oral hygiene, saliva, diet, tobacco exposure and individual susceptibility. Individual results vary. Oral hygiene, diet, general health, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, grinding, bite forces, material wear and attendance for maintenance can alter longevity. Even a satisfactory result may later need adjustment, repair, retreatment or replacement.

### FAQ 7

Question: What are the alternatives to teeth cleaning and polishing?

Answer:

Alternatives depend on the diagnosis and may include Routine Dental Check-up, Deep Dental Cleaning, Scaling and Root Planing. Monitoring or no immediate treatment may also be reasonable in selected situations. Options differ in invasiveness, reversibility, cost, maintenance, appearance and expected function. No one approach is universally superior, so the comparison must be based on the individual findings and informed preferences.

### FAQ 8

Question: What affects the cost of teeth cleaning and polishing?

Answer:

Cost may depend on assessment complexity, the number of teeth or areas, diagnostic imaging, materials, laboratory work, clinician or specialist involvement, anaesthesia, number of visits, additional procedures and maintenance requirements. Titanium Roots has not supplied a verified fee, so the CMS must display “Consultation required” and avoid publishing a numerical amount until formally approved.

### Treatment Overview

Treatment overview:

Dental Fillings is a dental procedure or care pathway that repairs a cavitated lesion or limited tooth defect with a direct restorative material selected for the clinical situation. It may be considered for concerns including cavitated decay, lost fillings, defective restorations, small fractures, localised wear, food trapping. The exact indication must be confirmed through history-taking, clinical examination and any justified diagnostic records.

Assessment commonly reviews symptoms, dental and medical history, medicines, allergies, oral hygiene, gum health, remaining tooth structure, bite and patient priorities. Where relevant, the clinician may discuss composite, glass-ionomer and other clinically appropriate direct materials; repair or replacement. Tests, photographs, scans or dental radiographs should be requested only when they are clinically justified and available at the clinic.

Very early non-cavitated disease may sometimes be managed non-restoratively, while extensive structural loss or pulpal disease may require an inlay, onlay, crown, root canal treatment or extraction rather than a direct repair.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Post-operative sensitivity, high bite, recurrent decay, fracture, pulpal inflammation and future replacement are possible. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

Website information cannot diagnose an individual or confirm suitability. A registered dental practitioner must review the clinical findings before treatment is recommended, and clinic-specific equipment, materials, practitioner availability and protocols must be verified before this page is published.

## Treatment Details

### Typical Appointment Duration

Approximately 30–90 minutes per tooth or appointment. This is an estimate rather than a guaranteed appointment length.

### Typical Number of Visits

Often one visit for a direct restoration; complex or staged care may require additional visits. The final sequence depends on diagnostic findings, response to treatment and the agreed plan.

### Anaesthesia or Sedation

Local anaesthesia is commonly used when tooth preparation may cause discomfort. Sedation is not routinely required and availability must be confirmed. No sedation service is claimed for Titanium Roots unless availability is separately verified.

### Benefits

* Title: Restores the defect
* Description: Replaces a limited area of missing or diseased tooth structure within the limits of the restoration.
* Sort order: 1

* Title: Supports function
* Description: Re-establishes a usable tooth shape for biting, chewing and cleaning.
* Sort order: 2

* Title: Seals a prepared area
* Description: Helps isolate the treated defect from food and oral bacteria while the restoration remains intact.
* Sort order: 3

* Title: Conservative option
* Description: May preserve more natural tooth structure than a full-coverage restoration when suitably indicated.
* Sort order: 4

* Title: Treatment choice
* Description: Allows material and design to be selected according to the tooth, defect, bite and appearance.
* Sort order: 5

* Title: Repair potential
* Description: Some localised defects may be repairable instead of requiring complete replacement.
* Sort order: 6

### Expected Outcome

The intended outcome is to repairs a cavitated lesion or limited tooth defect with a direct restorative material selected for the clinical situation within the biological and technical limits identified during assessment. Improvement may relate to health, comfort, function, appearance or maintenance, depending on the purpose of dental fillings.

Results are not guaranteed. Post-operative sensitivity, high bite, recurrent decay, fracture, pulpal inflammation and future replacement are possible. The outcome depends on diagnosis, anatomy, material or appliance selection, clinician technique, oral hygiene, general health, habits, attendance and long-term maintenance. Additional treatment, repair, review or referral may be required.

### Expected Longevity

Many direct restorations function for approximately 5–15 years, but some fail earlier and others last longer. Size, material, bite, moisture control, oral hygiene and maintenance strongly affect longevity.

For dental fillings, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving cavitated decay, lost fillings, defective restorations, small fractures, localised wear, food trapping.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Insufficient sound tooth structure — an indirect restoration or extraction may be more appropriate.
* Irreversible pulpal inflammation or infection — root canal treatment or extraction may be required.
* A substantial crack extending beyond a predictable direct repair — requires alternative planning.
* Inability to obtain suitable moisture control for the selected material — another material or technique may be needed.
* Uncontrolled caries risk or poor plaque control — a relative contraindication because recurrent decay risk is higher.
* Confirmed material allergy or sensitivity — avoid the relevant material.
* Medical instability — delay elective treatment or obtain clearance.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Alternative Treatments

* **Tooth-Coloured Fillings**  
  A restorative option that differs in coverage, material, preparation, retention or laboratory involvement.

* **Root Canal Treatment**  
  A clinically relevant alternative or complementary pathway selected after diagnosis and comparison of risks, limitations and maintenance.

* **Dental Inlays and Onlays**  
  A restorative option that differs in coverage, material, preparation, retention or laboratory involvement.

## Patient Journey

### Before-Treatment Preparation

* Provide a complete dental and medical history, current medicines and known allergies.
* Describe the concerns related to dental fillings, including timing, triggers and previous treatment.
* Allow a clinical examination and only those diagnostic records that are justified.
* Discuss reasonable alternatives, expected benefits, recognised risks and the option of no immediate treatment.
* Address active decay, gum disease or poor plaque control before elective definitive care where relevant.
* Inform the clinician about pregnancy, bleeding risk, smoking or nicotine use and previous treatment complications.
* Clarify appointment sequence, aftercare, maintenance responsibilities and factors affecting cost.
* Provide informed consent only after questions have been answered.

### Procedure Steps

A typical treatment pathway may include:

1. **Clinical assessment**  
   The tooth, symptoms, defect, remaining structure and bite are evaluated.

2. **Diagnostic decision**  
   Appropriate tests and justified imaging help determine lesion depth and pulpal status.

3. **Treatment and material selection**  
   A direct or other restoration is chosen according to the clinical situation.

4. **Anaesthesia and isolation**  
   Local anaesthesia may be used and the tooth is isolated as required.

5. **Defect management**  
   Diseased or unsupported tissue is managed conservatively according to the diagnosis.

6. **Restoration placement**  
   The selected material is inserted, adapted and set or cured.

7. **Finishing**  
   The restoration is shaped, smoothed and checked for cleanability and contact.

8. **Bite and aftercare**  
   Occlusion is checked and the patient receives recovery and maintenance instructions.

### Recovery and Downtime

Most patients return to routine activity after the visit. Numbness may last for several hours after local anaesthesia. The tooth may be temporarily sensitive to cold or pressure, and the jaw may feel tired after a longer appointment.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

### Risks and Limitations

Sensitivity, high bite, wear, marginal staining, recurrent decay, fracture, pulpal inflammation and future repair or replacement are recognised possibilities. Post-operative sensitivity, high bite, recurrent decay, fracture, pulpal inflammation and future replacement are possible.

The procedure may not achieve every intended functional or aesthetic objective. Biological response, anatomy, material limitations, patient cooperation and maintenance affect results. Future review, repair, retreatment, replacement or referral may be required.

### Aftercare

* Avoid chewing until numbness has reduced sufficiently to prevent injury.
* Follow material-specific eating instructions.
* Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste.
* Clean between the restored tooth and neighbouring teeth.
* Avoid repeatedly biting very hard objects.
* Reduce frequent sugary food and drink exposure.
* Attend reviews so the restoration and surrounding tooth can be monitored.
* Report a high bite, increasing pain or a loose restoration.

### When to Contact the Clinic

Contact the treating clinic for:

* Increasing pain rather than gradual improvement.
* Persistent or rapidly increasing swelling.
* Fever, discharge, a bad taste or other signs of infection.
* Prolonged or difficult-to-control bleeding.
* A loose, broken or lost restoration, appliance or prosthesis.
* A bite that feels significantly abnormal.
* Numbness or altered sensation lasting longer than expected.

Rapidly increasing facial swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe trauma, fever with spreading infection or uncontrolled bleeding may require urgent medical or dental care. This does not imply that Titanium Roots provides emergency or 24-hour services.

### When to Book a Consultation

Arrange a professional assessment when concerns involving cavitated decay, lost fillings, defective restorations, small fractures, localised wear, food trapping are present, when symptoms persist or when you want to understand whether dental fillings is appropriate. A dentist must examine the relevant teeth, gums, bite or supporting tissues before recommending care. Contact Titanium Roots Dental Clinic to arrange a consultation.

Tell the treating clinician about anxiety, previous difficult experiences or discomfort so that the procedure and support can be adjusted where clinically possible.

## Basic Information

Tooth-Coloured Fillings

### Short Description

Character count: 120/220

### Treatment Overview

Treatment overview:

Tooth-Coloured Fillings is a dental procedure or care pathway that uses an aesthetic direct material, commonly resin composite, to restore a suitable cavity or limited defect while blending with nearby tooth structure. It may be considered for concerns including small to moderate cavities, visible defective restorations, minor fractures, aesthetic direct restoration needs. The exact indication must be confirmed through history-taking, clinical examination and any justified diagnostic records.

Assessment commonly reviews symptoms, dental and medical history, medicines, allergies, oral hygiene, gum health, remaining tooth structure, bite and patient priorities. Where relevant, the clinician may discuss resin composite, glass-ionomer in selected sites, localised repair. Tests, photographs, scans or dental radiographs should be requested only when they are clinically justified and available at the clinic.

Very early non-cavitated disease may sometimes be managed non-restoratively, while extensive structural loss or pulpal disease may require an inlay, onlay, crown, root canal treatment or extraction rather than a direct repair.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Colour matching is approximate; staining, marginal wear, chipping, sensitivity and recurrent decay can occur. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

Website information cannot diagnose an individual or confirm suitability. A registered dental practitioner must review the clinical findings before treatment is recommended, and clinic-specific equipment, materials, practitioner availability and protocols must be verified before this page is published.

## Treatment Details

### Typical Appointment Duration

Approximately 30–90 minutes per tooth or appointment. This is an estimate rather than a guaranteed appointment length.

### Typical Number of Visits

Often one visit for a direct restoration; complex or staged care may require additional visits. The final sequence depends on diagnostic findings, response to treatment and the agreed plan.

### Anaesthesia or Sedation

Local anaesthesia is commonly used when tooth preparation may cause discomfort. Sedation is not routinely required and availability must be confirmed. No sedation service is claimed for Titanium Roots unless availability is separately verified.

### Benefits

* Title: Restores the defect
* Description: Replaces a limited area of missing or diseased tooth structure within the limits of the restoration.
* Sort order: 1

* Title: Supports function
* Description: Re-establishes a usable tooth shape for biting, chewing and cleaning.
* Sort order: 2

* Title: Seals a prepared area
* Description: Helps isolate the treated defect from food and oral bacteria while the restoration remains intact.
* Sort order: 3

* Title: Conservative option
* Description: May preserve more natural tooth structure than a full-coverage restoration when suitably indicated.
* Sort order: 4

* Title: Treatment choice
* Description: Allows material and design to be selected according to the tooth, defect, bite and appearance.
* Sort order: 5

* Title: Repair potential
* Description: Some localised defects may be repairable instead of requiring complete replacement.
* Sort order: 6

### Expected Outcome

The intended outcome is to uses an aesthetic direct material, commonly resin composite, to restore a suitable cavity or limited defect while blending with nearby tooth structure within the biological and technical limits identified during assessment. Improvement may relate to health, comfort, function, appearance or maintenance, depending on the purpose of tooth-coloured fillings.

Results are not guaranteed. Colour matching is approximate; staining, marginal wear, chipping, sensitivity and recurrent decay can occur. The outcome depends on diagnosis, anatomy, material or appliance selection, clinician technique, oral hygiene, general health, habits, attendance and long-term maintenance. Additional treatment, repair, review or referral may be required.

### Expected Longevity

Many direct restorations function for approximately 5–15 years, but some fail earlier and others last longer. Size, material, bite, moisture control, oral hygiene and maintenance strongly affect longevity.

For tooth-coloured fillings, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving small to moderate cavities, visible defective restorations, minor fractures, aesthetic direct restoration needs.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Insufficient sound tooth structure — an indirect restoration or extraction may be more appropriate.
* Irreversible pulpal inflammation or infection — root canal treatment or extraction may be required.
* A substantial crack extending beyond a predictable direct repair — requires alternative planning.
* Inability to obtain suitable moisture control for the selected material — another material or technique may be needed.
* Uncontrolled caries risk or poor plaque control — a relative contraindication because recurrent decay risk is higher.
* Confirmed material allergy or sensitivity — avoid the relevant material.
* Medical instability — delay elective treatment or obtain clearance.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Alternative Treatments

* **Dental Fillings**  
  A restorative option that differs in coverage, material, preparation, retention or laboratory involvement.

* **Composite Bonding**  
  A restorative option that differs in coverage, material, preparation, retention or laboratory involvement.

* **Dental Inlays and Onlays**  
  A restorative option that differs in coverage, material, preparation, retention or laboratory involvement.

## Patient Journey

### Before-Treatment Preparation

* Provide a complete dental and medical history, current medicines and known allergies.
* Describe the concerns related to tooth-coloured fillings, including timing, triggers and previous treatment.
* Allow a clinical examination and only those diagnostic records that are justified.
* Discuss reasonable alternatives, expected benefits, recognised risks and the option of no immediate treatment.
* Address active decay, gum disease or poor plaque control before elective definitive care where relevant.
* Inform the clinician about pregnancy, bleeding risk, smoking or nicotine use and previous treatment complications.
* Clarify appointment sequence, aftercare, maintenance responsibilities and factors affecting cost.
* Provide informed consent only after questions have been answered.

### Procedure Steps

A typical treatment pathway may include:

1. **Clinical assessment**  
   The tooth, symptoms, defect, remaining structure and bite are evaluated.

2. **Diagnostic decision**  
   Appropriate tests and justified imaging help determine lesion depth and pulpal status.

3. **Treatment and material selection**  
   A direct or other restoration is chosen according to the clinical situation.

4. **Anaesthesia and isolation**  
   Local anaesthesia may be used and the tooth is isolated as required.

5. **Defect management**  
   Diseased or unsupported tissue is managed conservatively according to the diagnosis.

6. **Restoration placement**  
   The selected material is inserted, adapted and set or cured.

7. **Finishing**  
   The restoration is shaped, smoothed and checked for cleanability and contact.

8. **Bite and aftercare**  
   Occlusion is checked and the patient receives recovery and maintenance instructions.

### Recovery and Downtime

Most patients return to routine activity after the visit. Numbness may last for several hours after local anaesthesia. The tooth may be temporarily sensitive to cold or pressure, and the jaw may feel tired after a longer appointment.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

### Risks and Limitations

Sensitivity, high bite, wear, marginal staining, recurrent decay, fracture, pulpal inflammation and future repair or replacement are recognised possibilities. Colour matching is approximate; staining, marginal wear, chipping, sensitivity and recurrent decay can occur.

The procedure may not achieve every intended functional or aesthetic objective. Biological response, anatomy, material limitations, patient cooperation and maintenance affect results. Future review, repair, retreatment, replacement or referral may be required.

### Aftercare

* Avoid chewing until numbness has reduced sufficiently to prevent injury.
* Follow material-specific eating instructions.
* Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste.
* Clean between the restored tooth and neighbouring teeth.
* Avoid repeatedly biting very hard objects.
* Reduce frequent sugary food and drink exposure.
* Attend reviews so the restoration and surrounding tooth can be monitored.
* Report a high bite, increasing pain or a loose restoration.

### When to Contact the Clinic

Contact the treating clinic for:

* Increasing pain rather than gradual improvement.
* Persistent or rapidly increasing swelling.
* Fever, discharge, a bad taste or other signs of infection.
* Prolonged or difficult-to-control bleeding.
* A loose, broken or lost restoration, appliance or prosthesis.
* A bite that feels significantly abnormal.
* Numbness or altered sensation lasting longer than expected.

Rapidly increasing facial swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe trauma, fever with spreading infection or uncontrolled bleeding may require urgent medical or dental care. This does not imply that Titanium Roots provides emergency or 24-hour services.

### When to Book a Consultation

Arrange a professional assessment when concerns involving small to moderate cavities, visible defective restorations, minor fractures, aesthetic direct restoration needs are present, when symptoms persist or when you want to understand whether tooth-coloured fillings is appropriate. A dentist must examine the relevant teeth, gums, bite or supporting tissues before recommending care. Contact Titanium Roots Dental Clinic to arrange a consultation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### FAQ 1

Question: What is Tooth-Coloured Fillings?

Answer:

Tooth-Coloured Fillings uses an aesthetic direct material, commonly resin composite, to restore a suitable cavity or limited defect while blending with nearby tooth structure. It may be considered for small to moderate cavities, visible defective restorations, minor fractures, aesthetic direct restoration needs, but the name of a treatment does not confirm that it is suitable for a particular person. The dentist must review symptoms, medical and dental history, clinical findings and any justified diagnostic records. The recommended approach may include resin composite, glass-ionomer in selected sites, localised repair.

### FAQ 2

Question: Is tooth-coloured fillings painful?

Answer:

Comfort varies with the condition being treated and the steps required. Local anaesthesia is commonly used when tooth preparation may cause discomfort. Sedation is not routinely required and availability must be confirmed. Pressure, vibration, temporary tenderness or sensitivity may still occur, and no responsible page can promise completely painless care. Tell the treating clinician about anxiety, previous difficult experiences or discomfort so that the procedure and support can be adjusted where clinically possible.

### FAQ 3

Question: How long does tooth-coloured fillings take?

Answer:

A typical estimate is approximately 30–90 minutes per tooth or appointment, but this is not guaranteed. Time varies with the number of teeth or areas involved, anatomy, disease severity, records, anaesthesia, cooperation, material or appliance selection and whether unexpected findings change the plan. Complex treatment should not be shortened merely to meet an advertised appointment time.

### FAQ 4

Question: How many visits are required for tooth-coloured fillings?

Answer:

Often one visit for a direct restoration; complex or staged care may require additional visits. Additional visits may be needed for diagnostic records, disease stabilisation, laboratory stages, healing, adjustment, review or management of complications. The dentist should explain the anticipated sequence after examination, while making clear that the plan can change if clinical findings or healing differ from expectations.

### FAQ 5

Question: Who may be suitable for tooth-coloured fillings?

Answer:

Possible candidates have a confirmed indication involving small to moderate cavities, visible defective restorations, minor fractures, aesthetic direct restoration needs, acceptable medical and oral-health conditions, and realistic expectations about benefits and limitations. Suitability may also depend on age, growth, tooth structure, gum or bone support, hygiene, smoking, medicines and ability to attend maintenance. A website description cannot replace a clinical assessment.

### FAQ 6

Question: How long do the results of tooth-coloured fillings last?

Answer:

Many direct restorations function for approximately 5–15 years, but some fail earlier and others last longer. Size, material, bite, moisture control, oral hygiene and maintenance strongly affect longevity. Individual results vary. Oral hygiene, diet, general health, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, grinding, bite forces, material wear and attendance for maintenance can alter longevity. Even a satisfactory result may later need adjustment, repair, retreatment or replacement.

### FAQ 7

Question: What are the alternatives to tooth-coloured fillings?

Answer:

Alternatives depend on the diagnosis and may include Dental Fillings, Composite Bonding, Dental Inlays and Onlays. Monitoring or no immediate treatment may also be reasonable in selected situations. Options differ in invasiveness, reversibility, cost, maintenance, appearance and expected function. No one approach is universally superior, so the comparison must be based on the individual findings and informed preferences.

### FAQ 8

Question: What affects the cost of tooth-coloured fillings?

Answer:

Cost may depend on assessment complexity, the number of teeth or areas, diagnostic imaging, materials, laboratory work, clinician or specialist involvement, anaesthesia, number of visits, additional procedures and maintenance requirements. Titanium Roots has not supplied a verified fee, so the CMS must display “Consultation required” and avoid publishing a numerical amount until formally approved.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

## Treatment Details

### Typical Appointment Duration

Approximately 20–45 minutes. This is an estimate rather than a guaranteed appointment length.

### Typical Number of Visits

Usually one visit, with recall based on individual risk and findings. The final sequence depends on diagnostic findings, response to treatment and the agreed plan.

### Anaesthesia or Sedation

Preventive assessment commonly requires no anaesthesia. Local anaesthesia may be considered only for a separately planned procedure. No sedation service is claimed for Titanium Roots unless availability is separately verified.

### Benefits

* Title: Risk reduction
* Description: Supports prevention or early management when the procedure is appropriate for the person’s current risk.
* Sort order: 1

* Title: Conservative care
* Description: Aims to preserve healthy tooth structure and avoid unnecessary intervention where possible.
* Sort order: 2

* Title: Targeted protection
* Description: Focuses preventive measures on surfaces or circumstances that are more susceptible to disease.
* Sort order: 3

* Title: Personalised advice
* Description: Links professional care with brushing, interdental cleaning, fluoride exposure and diet.
* Sort order: 4

* Title: Monitoring
* Description: Provides a baseline for reviewing changes and deciding whether further treatment is needed.
* Sort order: 5

* Title: Maintenance support
* Description: Works alongside regular self-care rather than replacing it.
* Sort order: 6

### Expected Outcome

The intended outcome is to applies a professionally selected topical fluoride product to strengthen susceptible tooth surfaces and reduce caries risk within the biological and technical limits identified during assessment. Improvement may relate to health, comfort, function, appearance or maintenance, depending on the purpose of professional fluoride treatment.

Results are not guaranteed. Temporary taste, coating or mild mucosal irritation can occur; product and dose must match age and risk. The outcome depends on diagnosis, anatomy, material or appliance selection, clinician technique, oral hygiene, general health, habits, attendance and long-term maintenance. Additional treatment, repair, review or referral may be required.

### Expected Longevity

Preventive benefit depends on ongoing home care, risk control and attendance at an individualised review interval.

For professional fluoride treatment, the clinically relevant duration also depends on the original condition, treatment design, material or appliance wear, bite forces, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, oral hygiene, general health and attendance for review. Results vary, and repair, adjustment, retreatment or replacement may be needed.

### Who Is This Treatment Suitable For?

* People with a clinically confirmed indication involving elevated decay risk, early non-cavitated lesions, exposed root surfaces, orthodontic appliances, dry mouth, recurrent decay.
* Patients whose dental and medical history allows the procedure to be carried out with an acceptable risk.
* People with oral hygiene and disease control appropriate to the proposed treatment.
* Patients with sufficient tooth, gum, bone or anatomical support where the procedure requires it.
* People able to understand the benefits, limitations, alternatives and maintenance commitment.
* Patients willing to attend diagnostic, treatment and review appointments.
* People with realistic expectations about comfort, appearance, duration and longevity.
* Patients whose age and growth status are compatible with the proposed procedure.

### Unsuitable Candidates or Contraindications

* Active cavitated disease requiring restorative care — preventive treatment alone may be insufficient.
* Uncontrolled gum disease — requires periodontal assessment alongside preventive measures.
* Allergy or sensitivity to the proposed product — select an alternative material.
* Inability to maintain basic oral hygiene — increases ongoing risk and requires tailored support.
* Medical instability — delay elective care or obtain clearance where relevant.
* Unrealistic expectation that prevention removes all future disease risk — address through informed discussion.

These factors are not automatically absolute contraindications. Their significance depends on severity, control, timing, available alternatives and clinical or medical assessment.

### Alternative Treatments

* **Routine Dental Check-up**  
  A diagnostic or preventive assessment used when further examination is needed before selecting a procedure.

* **Dental Sealants**  
  A preventive approach that may be more conservative when the tooth or patient remains suitable.

* **Tooth Sensitivity Treatment**  
  A clinically relevant alternative or complementary pathway selected after diagnosis and comparison of risks, limitations and maintenance.

## Patient Journey

### Before-Treatment Preparation

* Provide a complete dental and medical history, current medicines and known allergies.
* Describe the concerns related to professional fluoride treatment, including timing, triggers and previous treatment.
* Allow a clinical examination and only those diagnostic records that are justified.
* Discuss reasonable alternatives, expected benefits, recognised risks and the option of no immediate treatment.
* Address active decay, gum disease or poor plaque control before elective definitive care where relevant.
* Inform the clinician about pregnancy, bleeding risk, smoking or nicotine use and previous treatment complications.
* Clarify appointment sequence, aftercare, maintenance responsibilities and factors affecting cost.
* Provide informed consent only after questions have been answered.

### Procedure Steps

A typical treatment pathway may include:

1. **Risk assessment**  
   The clinician reviews previous disease, hygiene, diet, fluoride exposure and relevant medical factors.

2. **Clinical examination**  
   Susceptible teeth or surfaces are inspected to confirm whether preventive care is appropriate.

3. **Disease-status check**  
   Active cavitation, gum disease or another condition requiring treatment is identified before prevention proceeds.

4. **Product or technique selection**  
   The preventive material, concentration, surface or method is selected for the individual indication.

5. **Isolation and preparation**  
   The treatment area is cleaned and controlled as required for the selected product.

6. **Application**  
   The preventive material is placed according to its clinical instructions.

7. **Quality check**  
   Coverage, retention or treated surfaces are reviewed.

8. **Home-care and recall**  
   The clinician explains daily care, diet, fluoride use and when the result should be reassessed.

### Recovery and Downtime

Most preventive procedures cause little or no downtime. Temporary taste, surface roughness, mild gum contact or brief sensitivity may occur depending on the product. Eating and drinking instructions vary with the material used and should be followed exactly.

Recovery differs between patients. Any procedure-specific eating, activity, cleaning, appliance or medicine instructions must come from the treating clinician.

### Risks and Limitations

Preventive measures reduce risk but cannot guarantee that decay or gum disease will not occur, and treated surfaces still require daily care and monitoring. Temporary taste, coating or mild mucosal irritation can occur; product and dose must match age and risk.

The procedure may not achieve every intended functional or aesthetic objective. Biological response, anatomy, material limitations, patient cooperation and maintenance affect results. Future review, repair, retreatment, replacement or referral may be required.

### Aftercare

* Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste as advised.
* Clean between teeth using an appropriate method.
* Follow dietary advice aimed at reducing frequent sugar exposure.
* Avoid tobacco and areca-nut use.
* Attend the recommended risk-based review.
* Monitor treated surfaces or risk areas for change.
* Use additional fluoride products only when recommended by a clinician.

### When to Contact the Clinic

Contact the treating clinic for:

* Increasing pain rather than gradual improvement.
* Persistent or rapidly increasing swelling.
* Fever, discharge, a bad taste or other signs of infection.
* Prolonged or difficult-to-control bleeding.
* A loose, broken or lost restoration, appliance or prosthesis.
* A bite that feels significantly abnormal.
* Numbness or altered sensation lasting longer than expected.

Rapidly increasing facial swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe trauma, fever with spreading infection or uncontrolled bleeding may require urgent medical or dental care. This does not imply that Titanium Roots provides emergency or 24-hour services.

### When to Book a Consultation

Arrange a professional assessment when concerns involving elevated decay risk, early non-cavitated lesions, exposed root surfaces, orthodontic appliances, dry mouth, recurrent decay are present, when symptoms persist or when you want to understand whether professional fluoride treatment is appropriate. A dentist must examine the relevant teeth, gums, bite or supporting tissues before recommending care. Contact Titanium Roots Dental Clinic to arrange a consultation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### FAQ 1

Question: What is Professional Fluoride Treatment?

Answer:

Professional Fluoride Treatment applies a professionally selected topical fluoride product to strengthen susceptible tooth surfaces and reduce caries risk. It may be considered for elevated decay risk, early non-cavitated lesions, exposed root surfaces, orthodontic appliances, dry mouth, recurrent decay, but the name of a treatment does not confirm that it is suitable for a particular person. The dentist must review symptoms, medical and dental history, clinical findings and any justified diagnostic records. The recommended approach may include fluoride varnish, gel, foam or another professionally indicated formulation.

### FAQ 2

Question: Is professional fluoride treatment painful?

Answer:

Comfort varies with the condition being treated and the steps required. Preventive assessment commonly requires no anaesthesia. Local anaesthesia may be considered only for a separately planned procedure. Pressure, vibration, temporary tenderness or sensitivity may still occur, and no responsible page can promise completely painless care. Tell the treating clinician about anxiety, previous difficult experiences or discomfort so that the procedure and support can be adjusted where clinically possible.

### FAQ 3

Question: How long does professional fluoride treatment take?

Answer:

A typical estimate is approximately 20–45 minutes, but this is not guaranteed. Time varies with the number of teeth or areas involved, anatomy, disease severity, records, anaesthesia, cooperation, material or appliance selection and whether unexpected findings change the plan. Complex treatment should not be shortened merely to meet an advertised appointment time.

### FAQ 4

Question: How many visits are required for professional fluoride treatment?

Answer:

Usually one visit, with recall based on individual risk and findings. Additional visits may be needed for diagnostic records, disease stabilisation, laboratory stages, healing, adjustment, review or management of complications. The dentist should explain the anticipated sequence after examination, while making clear that the plan can change if clinical findings or healing differ from expectations.

### FAQ 5

Question: Who may be suitable for professional fluoride treatment?

Answer:

Possible candidates have a confirmed indication involving elevated decay risk, early non-cavitated lesions, exposed root surfaces, orthodontic appliances, dry mouth, recurrent decay, acceptable medical and oral-health conditions, and realistic expectations about benefits and limitations. Suitability may also depend on age, growth, tooth structure, gum or bone support, hygiene, smoking, medicines and ability to attend maintenance. A website description cannot replace a clinical assessment.

### FAQ 6

Question: How long do the results of professional fluoride treatment last?

Answer:

Preventive benefit depends on ongoing home care, risk control and attendance at an individualised review interval. Individual results vary. Oral hygiene, diet, general health, smoking or nicotine exposure where relevant, grinding, bite forces, material wear and attendance for maintenance can alter longevity. Even a satisfactory result may later need adjustment, repair, retreatment or replacement.

### FAQ 7

Question: What are the alternatives to professional fluoride treatment?

Answer:

Alternatives depend on the diagnosis and may include Routine Dental Check-up, Dental Sealants, Tooth Sensitivity Treatment. Monitoring or no immediate treatment may also be reasonable in selected situations. Options differ in invasiveness, reversibility, cost, maintenance, appearance and expected function. No one approach is universally superior, so the comparison must be based on the individual findings and informed preferences.

### FAQ 8

Question: What affects the cost of professional fluoride treatment?

Answer:

Cost may depend on assessment complexity, the number of teeth or areas, diagnostic imaging, materials, laboratory work, clinician or specialist involvement, anaesthesia, number of visits, additional procedures and maintenance requirements. Titanium Roots has not supplied a verified fee, so the CMS must display “Consultation required” and avoid publishing a numerical amount until formally approved.

### Treatment Overview

Treatment overview:

Dental Sealants is a dental procedure or care pathway that places a protective material into susceptible pits and fissures to reduce plaque retention and caries risk on selected teeth. It may be considered for concerns including deep grooves, elevated pit-and-fissure caries risk, newly erupted molars, suitable early non-cavitated lesions. The exact indication must be confirmed through history-taking, clinical examination and any justified diagnostic records.

Assessment commonly reviews symptoms, dental and medical history, medicines, allergies, oral hygiene, gum health, remaining tooth structure, bite and patient priorities. Where relevant, the clinician may discuss resin-based sealant, glass-ionomer sealant, preventive resin restoration where indicated. Tests, photographs, scans or dental radiographs should be requested only when they are clinically justified and available at the clinic.

The procedure is preventive rather than a substitute for daily plaque control. Its benefit depends on baseline risk, correct case selection, continued fluoride exposure where appropriate and review of changes over time.

A typical pathway includes explanation of the findings, comparison of reasonable alternatives, informed consent, treatment or monitoring and appropriate review. Sealants can wear, chip or detach and do not protect untreated smooth surfaces or replace daily plaque control. Appointment duration, number of visits, recovery, prognosis, longevity and cost vary with anatomy, disease severity, materials, general health, habits, maintenance and the final treatment plan.

Website information cannot diagnose an individual or confirm suitability. A registered dental practitioner must review the clinical findings before treatment is recommended, and clinic-specific equipment, materials, practitioner availability and protocols must be verified before this page is published.
